column35: See: Bardachd a Albainn Nuaidh, ed. Calum Macleod (1970), p. 42-43.

column2: A conversation with Joe Neil MacNeil about songs and stories
column33: A conversation about waulking songs, old songs, general songs and stories. Occasional verses are recited throughout. Some of the songs record local events, e.g. a fire that went out of control. Mention is made of the Currie bards, and other bards such as Donald MacIntyre (Dòmhnall Ruairidh Ailein). Stories and storytelling are examined, e.g. 'The Three Black Hats'.

column34:
Composed by Anna Gillies of Morar, who sailed from Greenock to Quebec on the 'MacDonald' in the autumn of 1786.
See: The Emigrant Experience, ed. Margaret MacDonell (1982), p. 132.

23 couplets with a refrain. Composed by a Campbell woman after the Covenanter defeat at the hands of Royalist Irish and Highlanders led by Alasdair MacColla.
column35: See: Songs Remembered in Exile, ed. John Lorne Campbell (1990), p. 205-6.

column33: In this song a man is lamenting what happened at the Battle of Inverlochy. A band of Irishmen came over to Scotland to fight with the MacDonalds. They killed his father, his wife and his children. They also killed his cattle and sheep and they ruined his oats and barley.
column34: Copy of Ediphone wax cylinder recording.
column35: See: Songs Remembered in Exile, ed. John Lorne Campbell (1990), p. 205-6.

column33: The woman who composed this song tells of her grief following the infamous Battle of Inverlochy. She describes how the Irish came to help the MacDonalds. Her father and husband, four young sons and nine foster children were killed. Her cattle were slaughtered, her sheep were roasted and her oats and barley were destroyed.
column34: Copied from Ediphone wax cylinder recording. Twelve lines sung. Each line is repeated. The song was composed by a Campbell woman after the Battle of Inverlochy in 1645, when the parliamentary forces under the Duke of Argyll were defeated by the Royalists under Montrose and Alasdair MacDonald.
column35: See: Songs Remembered in Exile, ed. John Lorne Campbell (1990), p. 205-6.

It is not easy for him to make a new life in a new country and he is missing what he left behind. People are going to the new country expecting an easier life but he says that they have been deceived.

He then wanted to kill the bear and he waited for him all night but the bear didn't appear. He then hung the dead lamb in the byre but when he awoke the next morning the bear had broken into the byre and had eaten the lamb.

The bard is very sad and he cannot even raise a tune.
